title: Classes and Objects: Bundle Data and Behavior Into One Thing
excerpt: Stop juggling loose dictionaries: see how a class bundles data and actions into objects you can create as many times as you like.

headings.text: Define a Class and Create Objects
Have You Been Using Classes All Along?

html:
Suppose you are writing a program about dogs. Each dog has a name and an age, and you want to do things with dogs: describe them, make them speak, track their birthdays. You can store the data in dictionaries and write separate functions, and for a small program that works. As the program grows, the data and the code that works on it drift apart.

A class is a blueprint that bundles related data and the actions on that data into one unit, and an object is a single thing built from that blueprint. This lesson builds the idea from the ground up, starting with the problem a class solves.

The Problem With Loose Data

Here is the dictionary approach. A dictionary stores labelled values, such as the name Rex under the label "name". Each dog is a dictionary, and a separate function describes any dog you give it (str() turns the age number into text so it can be joined to other text):

dog1 = {"name": "Rex", "age": 3}
dog2 = {"name": "Fido", "age": 5}

def describe(dog):
    return dog["name"] + " is " + str(dog["age"])

print(describe(dog1))
print(describe(dog2))
Rex is 3
Fido is 5

It works, but nothing ties the function to the dictionaries, and nothing stops a typo in a key from sneaking in:

print(dog1["nmae"])
KeyError: 'nmae'

The KeyError means you asked a dictionary for a key it does not have. Wouldn't it be better if the data and the code that uses it lived together, and every dog was guaranteed the same shape? That is exactly what a class gives you.

Define a Class and Create Objects

The keyword class defines a new type of thing. By convention, class names start with a capital letter. The smallest possible class has no content at all, which Python writes as pass:

class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()

print(type(rex))
print(isinstance(rex, Dog))
<class '__main__.Dog'>
True

Writing Dog() builds a new object from the blueprint. The variable rex is an object, also called an instance of Dog, and type() and isinstance() confirm it (__main__ in the output just means "defined in the file you are running"). Think of the class as a cookie cutter and the objects as the cookies: one cutter can make as many cookies as you like.

Objects Hold Their Own Data

Data stored on an object is called an attribute. You can attach attributes with a dot, and each object keeps its own:

rex.name = "Rex"
rex.age = 3

fido = Dog()
fido.name = "Fido"

print(rex.name, rex.age)
print(fido.name)
Rex 3
Fido

What happens if you ask for an attribute that was never set? Python tells you at once, instead of quietly returning nothing:

print(fido.age)
AttributeError: 'Dog' object has no attribute 'age'

Fido never received an age, so the lookup fails with an AttributeError, which means the object has no attribute with that name. Attaching attributes one at a time after creating an object is easy to forget.

Have You Been Using Classes All Along?

Yes. Every value in Python is an object of some class, including the numbers, strings and lists of everyday Python:

print(type(5), type("a"), type([1]))
<class 'int'> <class 'str'> <class 'list'>

So when you write "hello".upper() or [1, 2].append(3), you are using actions that belong to the str and list classes. Writing your own class lets you create types that fit your own problem.

Every Object Is Separate

Two objects built from the same class are different objects, even when they hold the same data. The word is asks whether two names point to the very same object, and == asks whether they are equal:

a = Dog()
b = Dog()

print(a is b)
print(a == b)
False
False

Both comparisons are False. By default, Python considers two objects equal only if they are the very same object.

Bundling Behavior: Your First Method

A class can also hold functions, which are called methods when they live inside a class. Here is a dog that can speak:

class Dog:
    def speak(self):
        return "Woof"

rex = Dog()
print(rex.speak())
Woof

What is self? It is the object the method was called on. When you write rex.speak(), Python passes rex to the method automatically as the first argument, which is why the definition has a parameter even though the call has none. That is how a method can reach the object's own data.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonClassesObjects.ipynb.

Summary

  • A class is a blueprint defined with class Name:; an object (instance) is one thing built from it with Name().
  • Class names conventionally start with a capital letter.
  • Data stored on an object is an attribute, read and set with a dot; each object has its own.
  • Reading an attribute that was never set raises an AttributeError.
  • Numbers, strings and lists are objects of built-in classes.
  • Two objects are equal by default only if they are the same object.
  • Functions inside a class are methods, and self is the object the method was called on.
